questions.question: A fintech platform stores database passwords, API keys, and TLS private keys scattered across config files, environment variables, and developer laptops. Audit trails are nonexistent and rotation is manual. They want centralised storage, fine-grained access control, leasing, and tamper-evident audit logs for sensitive material. Which problem does the product solve?
options: Acts as a high-throughput cache that stores sensitive configuration material with access logging and leasing, but without policy enforcement or dynamic credential generation
Centralises sensitive material with policy-based access, short-lived dynamic credentials, leasing, and an append-only audit log of every read
Replaces TLS certificate authorities with a managed root chain that signs end-entity certificates for browser-facing endpoints only
Provides a queue-based message bus that routes credential-rotation events between microservices in a fan-out broadcast pattern
questions.explanation: Vault solves secrets sprawl: it centralises secrets with policy-based access, dynamic credentials with leases, fine-grained ACLs, encryption as a service, and an append-only audit log. The cache description omits the core policy engine — Vault is not a cache. The PKI description is one engine inside Vault, not the product itself; Vault does far more than TLS. And Vault is not a message bus — it has no fan-out routing of rotation events between services.

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine generates real AWS IAM credentials with a configurable TTL that are automatically revoked on expiry?
options: Transit secrets engine — encrypts AWS keys at rest while leaving the underlying IAM user untouched
KV v2 secrets engine — stores AWS access keys as versioned static secrets with rotation metadata
Cubbyhole secrets engine — issues per-token AWS access keys scoped to the cubbyhole's TTL
AWS secrets engine — generates dynamic IAM access keys on demand and revokes them at lease expiry
questions.explanation: The AWS secrets engine generates dynamic IAM access keys on demand with a TTL: Vault creates the IAM credentials via the AWS API, hands them to the application, and deletes them when the lease expires. Transit is encryption-as-a-service — it does not create IAM users. KV v2 stores arbitrary static values; it has no idea what an IAM user is and cannot revoke one. Cubbyhole is a per-token private KV — it never creates IAM credentials and has no AWS integration.

questions.question: An application needs to authenticate to Vault without human interaction. Which auth method is specifically designed for machine-to-Vault authentication?
options: LDAP auth method — validates a username and password against a directory server
Userpass auth method — validates a username and password stored in Vault itself
AppRole auth method — uses a non-sensitive role_id and a separately delivered secret_id
GitHub auth method — validates a personal access token tied to a GitHub user account
questions.explanation: AppRole is purpose-built for automated pipelines and applications: a non-sensitive role_id can be embedded in the app, and a sensitive secret_id is delivered separately at deploy time, enforcing a two-factor pattern for machines. LDAP and Userpass both require a human username/password — they are designed for interactive operator login, not unattended workloads. GitHub auth requires a developer's personal access token, again a human credential.

questions.question: After any successful authentication against Vault (userpass, AppRole, AWS IAM, Kubernetes service account, OIDC, …) the client receives the same kind of object that carries TTL, policies, accessor, and metadata, and is presented on later API calls. Which object is returned?
options: A short-lived signed JWT bearing external identity claims with embedded policies, validated locally by each Vault node without any server lookup
A session cookie scoped to the auth method's mount path, kept only in the client's in-memory keyring and discarded on process exit
A token with TTL, policies, accessor, and metadata that the client presents in subsequent requests until revocation or expiry
A wrapped response handle that must be unwrapped exactly once before the actual credentials become usable to the workload
questions.explanation: Every Vault auth method returns a Vault token after a successful login. The token carries attached policies, a TTL, an accessor for administrative revocation, and metadata. It is the universal identity object used for every subsequent API call. Vault tokens are not JWTs and are not validated locally — they are looked up by each node against the storage backend (except batch tokens, which are still tokens, not JWTs). They are not session cookies. Response wrapping is an optional layer applied around a secret for delivery; it is not what every login returns by default.

questions.question: A platform team writes a policy attached to an app role. Inside the policy they declare which actions the holder may perform on each path. The set of allowed actions is fixed by Vault. Which set lists capabilities a policy can grant on a path?
options: create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny
get, post, put, patch, delete, head, options
select, insert, update, delete, execute, grant, revoke
allow, deny, audit, broadcast, suppress, escalate, override
questions.explanation: Vault policy capabilities are a fixed set: create (write new), read, update (overwrite existing), delete, list (enumerate keys), sudo (root-restricted operations), and deny (explicit deny that overrides any allow). The HTTP verbs (get/post/put…) are how the API is called, but policies do not name verbs — they name capabilities. SQL-style verbs (select/insert/grant) are database concepts, unrelated to Vault policies. The fictional allow/audit/broadcast/escalate list is not part of Vault's policy language.

questions.question: A team is choosing between two flavours of the static-secrets engine. One stores only the current value of each key. The other adds versioning, soft-delete, and metadata. What is the principal difference?
options: The newer flavour persists data on Raft while the older flavour only writes to the file backend and is unsuitable for production deployments
The newer flavour adds per-key versioning with configurable max-versions, soft-delete plus undelete, and per-key metadata
The newer flavour returns secrets in Protobuf while the older flavour only returns JSON, with the wire format negotiated at request time
Both flavours use the same audit log shape; the older flavour just requires an external syslog forwarder for compliance
questions.explanation: KV v2 is the versioned static-secrets engine: writing a new value preserves old versions (with a configurable max), soft-delete marks a version deleted but recoverable via undelete, and per-key metadata is supported. KV v1 silently overwrites and offers no recovery. KV v1 is not tied to the file backend — either KV version works with any storage backend, so storage is not the distinction. The two engines use the same JSON wire format, so the Protobuf claim is fabricated. Audit logging is configured at the Vault level, identical for both KV versions; the syslog-forwarder framing is invented.

questions.question: A microservice requests a database credential. Instead of being handed a long-lived password from a config file, it receives a freshly generated username and password whose lifetime is bound to a lease and which Vault will revoke when the lease expires. What is this called, and what is its principal advantage?
options: Dynamic secret — generated on demand with a TTL, unique per workload, auto-revoked on lease expiry so no shared long-lived password exists
Wrapped secret — Vault returns a one-time handle that the workload unwraps to obtain a pre-generated long-lived password from an operator
Response-signed secret — Vault attaches a JWT signature so callers verify provenance, but the credential itself is rotated by an external job
Static rotated secret — Vault stores the password unchanged and rotates it on a fixed schedule, notifying clients via a webhook ahead of the change
questions.explanation: Dynamic secrets are generated on demand (a real database user, an IAM key) with a TTL and auto-revoke on lease expiry — short-lived, unique per workload, and no manual rotation. Response wrapping is a delivery mechanism for an already-existing secret; the underlying credential is still whatever it was, not freshly generated per request. Response-signed secrets are not a Vault concept. Static rotated secrets exist (database static roles), but the credential is shared — the question describes a freshly generated per-request username/password, which is the dynamic-secret pattern.

questions.question: A Vault lease is about to expire. The application calls `vault lease renew`. What happens if the renewal would exceed the secret's `max_lease_ttl`?
options: Vault grants a renewal only up to the `max_lease_ttl` ceiling; beyond that the application must request a new secret
Vault revokes the secret immediately when the renewal request would otherwise exceed the ceiling
Vault converts the lease into a non-expiring permanent secret since the ceiling is treated as advisory
Vault allows the renewal and silently extends `max_lease_ttl` so renewal stays uninterrupted
questions.explanation: `max_lease_ttl` is a hard ceiling on the total lifetime of a lease. Vault will renew up to that ceiling but never past it — once reached, the application must request a fresh secret (which yields new credentials). It does not revoke the secret immediately on the renewal call; it shortens the renewal grant instead. There is no concept of a non-expiring lease in Vault — `max_lease_ttl` cannot be bypassed by a renewal call. And the ceiling itself is never silently extended; that would defeat the safety property the setting exists to provide.

questions.question: In AppRole authentication, which component is considered NON-sensitive and can be safely embedded in application code or configuration?
options: The wrapped response token that delivers the secret_id at deploy time
The role_id — analogous to a username; identifies the role without granting access
The secret_id — the sensitive shared secret that proves the workload's identity
The final Vault token issued after a successful AppRole login
questions.explanation: The role_id is analogous to a username: it names which role the workload claims to be but cannot authenticate on its own, so it can be embedded in application config. The secret_id is sensitive (the password half) and must be delivered separately, ideally via response wrapping at deploy time. The wrapped token transports the secret_id and is itself one-time-use and sensitive. The final Vault token issued post-login is a fully privileged credential — definitely sensitive.

questions.question: An application needs to encrypt sensitive data before storing it in a database but should NOT store the encryption keys itself. Which Vault secrets engine solves this?
options: PKI secrets engine — issues X.509 certificates; the app uses the resulting key pair to encrypt and decrypt records
Database secrets engine — wraps each value in a per-row encrypted column managed by the database plugin
KV v2 secrets engine — stores ciphertext alongside the data key, returning both on read so the app can decrypt
Transit secrets engine — encryption-as-a-service: the app sends plaintext and gets ciphertext, the key never leaves Vault
questions.explanation: Transit is encryption-as-a-service: the application sends plaintext, Vault returns ciphertext, and the key never leaves Vault. The app stores only ciphertext, and key rotation is supported (Vault can rewrap existing ciphertext). PKI issues TLS certificates for authenticating endpoints — it is not a data-at-rest encryption service. The Database engine creates dynamic database users; it does not encrypt arbitrary application data. KV v2 just stores arbitrary values — it cannot encrypt application payloads without exposing a key.

questions.question: A company wants to eliminate long-lived TLS certificates (valid 1–2 years). Which Vault secrets engine enables issuing short-lived certificates on demand?
options: KV v2 secrets engine — store pre-issued certificates with versioning and rotate by adding new versions
Transit secrets engine — issue signing keys that the application uses to mint certificates locally
PKI secrets engine — acts as an internal CA that issues short-lived X.509 certificates on demand
SSH secrets engine — signs SSH host and user certificates; can be repurposed to sign TLS endpoints
questions.explanation: The PKI secrets engine acts as an internal Certificate Authority and issues short-lived X.509 certificates on demand (TTL configurable from hours to days), so services request a fresh cert at startup and let it expire naturally. KV v2 only stores values; it does not issue certificates and the static certs it would hold are exactly the long-lived ones the team wants to remove. Transit can sign data, but it is not an X.509 CA and produces no usable end-entity TLS certificate. The SSH engine signs SSH credentials (not X.509) — it has no TLS issuance mode.

questions.question: A developer runs `vault read database/creds/my-role` and gets a username and password. What happens to those credentials when the Vault lease expires?
options: The credentials are archived in a database-specific KV mount for audit and forensic review by the security team
Vault sends an inbound notification to the application asking it to stop using the credentials immediately
The credentials remain valid indefinitely — the database has no idea about Vault, so the lease only affects Vault's metadata
Vault connects to the database and drops the user it created, revoking access at lease expiry
questions.explanation: The Database secrets engine creates real database users for the granted TTL. When the lease expires (or is revoked), Vault uses its stored admin connection to drop or disable that user — revocation is automatic and immediate at the database level. Vault does not archive credentials to a separate KV mount; the engine just removes the user. It does not push notifications to applications; expiry happens silently. The credentials are not indefinitely valid — the database does not know about Vault directly, but Vault holds the admin connection that lets it execute the revocation.

questions.question: Which Vault component runs as a client-side daemon, handles automatic authentication, and writes secrets to local files for applications to consume?
options: Vault Sentinel — policy-as-code engine that filters API requests against signed Sentinel rules
Vault Server — the central process that stores data on the configured backend and serves the API
Vault Proxy — a transparent forwarding proxy that requests are routed through to reach the active node
Vault Agent — client daemon that auto-authenticates, renews leases, and renders templated secrets to files
questions.explanation: Vault Agent is a client-side daemon: it handles auto-auth (AppRole, Kubernetes, AWS, …), renews tokens and leases, and uses templating to render secrets into config files so the application reads files instead of using a Vault SDK. Sentinel is the Enterprise policy-as-code engine that filters requests, not a client daemon that writes secrets. Vault Server is the central server process — the thing Agent talks to, not the daemon that renders files. Vault Proxy / vault proxy mode forwards API requests with caching, but it does not author template-rendered secret files for applications.

questions.question: A team uses response wrapping to deliver an AppRole secret_id to a new service. When the service goes to unwrap the token, it gets an error saying the token has already been used. What does this indicate?
options: Someone intercepted and unwrapped the token before the legitimate recipient — response wrapping is single-use, so re-use signals tampering
The service used the wrong Vault address and Vault rejected the unwrap call for that reason
The Vault server restarted and cleared all in-flight wrapping tokens, so the recipient sees a used-token error
The wrapping token expired due to clock skew between the deliverer and the recipient host
questions.explanation: Response wrapping is single-use: if an unwrap call reports the token has already been consumed, an interceptor unwrapped it first. This is a deliberate security feature so tampering is detectable. Wrong-address calls produce an unrelated connection error or 404, not a 'token already used' message. A server restart does not flag tokens as used — it simply makes them unknown. Expired wrapping tokens return an expiry error, again distinct from 'already used'. The right response is to investigate the delivery channel and revoke any secrets the interceptor may have obtained.

questions.question: A security-conscious operator configures multiple audit devices on a Vault cluster: file, syslog, and a remote socket. During a partial outage every audit device fails to write simultaneously. What does Vault do with in-flight requests?
options: Continues serving requests and queues audit records in memory for replay once any device recovers, accepting bounded loss on crash
Switches to a hot-standby node with independent audit devices, transparently retrying the request without affecting the client
Blocks all requests until at least one audit device acknowledges the write, so no operation proceeds without a durable audit record
Falls back to a degraded audit summary written to the storage backend, with a flag indicating reduced fidelity for compliance
questions.explanation: Vault prioritises audit integrity over availability: if every enabled audit device fails to write, Vault blocks all operations so it never executes silently. That is why operators enable multiple devices (file + syslog) — any single failure must not gate the whole cluster. Vault does not queue audit records in memory; that would mean operations completing without a durable audit trail. There is no failover to a standby with independent audit devices — audit-device configuration is cluster-wide. And Vault has no 'degraded audit summary' fallback on storage; the unaudited-state policy is fail-closed by design.

questions.question: A Vault server starts and is in 'sealed' state. What must happen before it can serve any requests?
options: The root token must be re-created using `vault operator init` again on the running cluster
The server must register with a HashiCorp-hosted license server before the seal can be lifted
A quorum of unseal key shares must be provided to reconstruct the master key and decrypt the data
The administrator must restart the Vault service with a special unseal flag set on the binary
questions.explanation: Vault uses Shamir's Secret Sharing to split the master key. Unsealing requires a quorum of key shares (default 3 of 5) to reconstruct the master key and decrypt the storage barrier. Auto-unseal (Cloud KMS or HSM) automates this for production but is still based on decrypting the master key. `vault operator init` can only be run once per cluster — it is not re-run on every restart. Vault OSS needs no license server (Enterprise validates a license file locally, not by phoning home, and a sealed Vault would not even reach that step). There is no special restart flag that unseals — unsealing is an API operation, not a launch argument.

questions.question: In a Vault HA cluster, a client sends a request to a standby node. What does the standby node do?
options: Promotes itself to active and processes the request locally, then steps back down once the call returns
Rejects the request with a 503 error and asks the client to look up the active node and retry
Processes the request locally using its cached read-only copy of the storage backend
Forwards the request to the active node transparently and returns the response to the client
questions.explanation: In Vault HA, only one node is active at a time. Standby nodes transparently forward requests to the active node and return its response, so from the client's perspective the request just succeeds regardless of which node was contacted. A standby does not promote itself for one request — leader elections happen only when the active node loses its lock. Standbys do not reject with 503 (that would defeat the point of putting a load balancer in front of them). And there is no read-only cache that standbys serve from — Vault does not split reads and writes across nodes.

questions.question: A team is choosing the storage backend for a production Vault cluster. They want minimal moving parts, no external dependencies, native HA, and snapshot/restore tooling. Which advantage favours the embedded Raft option over an external consensus store?
options: Raft supports more secrets engines and auth methods than other backends, because the embedded driver exposes a richer plugin enumeration interface
Raft removes the operational burden of running a separate consensus cluster — Vault manages its own storage and replication in-process
Raft writes plaintext data while other backends keep ciphertext that must be decrypted on read, so Raft is faster at read time
Raft is the only backend that supports cross-region replication, which other backends gate behind a paid tier
questions.explanation: Integrated Raft storage (Vault 1.4+) lets Vault manage its own consensus and replication in-process, eliminating the need to run Consul or another external cluster — fewer moving parts, simpler operations, and it is the recommended default for new deployments. Raft does not enable more secrets engines or auth methods than other backends; engine availability is independent of storage. All backends store Vault's barrier-encrypted ciphertext, never plaintext, so the read-speed framing is wrong. Cross-region replication is a Vault Enterprise feature gated by edition, not by storage backend choice.

questions.question: A user authenticates to Vault via LDAP and also via GitHub. How does Vault's identity system track this as the same person?
options: Only the most recently used auth method is considered active; older sessions are silently invalidated by Vault
Vault cannot correlate logins across different auth methods — each method creates an isolated identity
Vault Identity creates a single Entity with one Alias per auth method, so both logins resolve to the same Entity
The user must manually link their LDAP and GitHub accounts in the Vault UI before any correlation occurs
questions.explanation: Vault Identity represents each unique user or workload as an Entity, and each auth method login creates an Alias linked to that Entity. Both the LDAP alias and the GitHub alias resolve to the same Entity, so any policy attached to the Entity applies regardless of how the user logged in. Vault does not silently invalidate older sessions on a new login — both tokens stay valid until they hit TTL or revocation. Vault absolutely can correlate logins across methods (that is the whole point of the Identity system). Manual linking via the UI is one way to merge aliases for an Entity, but auto-grouping by Identity already handles the common case; correlation is not gated on a UI step.

questions.question: Vault Namespaces is a feature that allows multi-tenant deployments within a single cluster. Which Vault edition includes Namespaces?
options: Vault Enterprise — and HCP Vault, which runs the Enterprise binary under the hood
Vault OSS (open-source) on Linux, gated by a feature flag set at server startup
Vault Community Edition with a published HCL stanza enabling tenant isolation
All Vault editions including the free self-hosted tier and Community Edition
questions.explanation: Vault Namespaces is an Enterprise-only feature — each namespace has its own auth methods, secrets engines, policies, and tokens inside one cluster, supporting Vault-as-a-Service for multiple teams. HCP Vault includes namespaces because it runs the Enterprise binary; that does not make namespaces free. Vault OSS (now Community Edition) does not include namespaces — there is no feature-flag toggle in the open-source binary. Community Edition similarly has no HCL stanza for tenant isolation. And there is no free tier that includes namespaces — every tier that has them is a paid Enterprise edition.

questions.question: A pod running in a managed cluster needs to read database credentials from Vault. It has no pre-provisioned token or static API key — only its service-account JWT projected into the filesystem. Which auth method lets it authenticate using that JWT?
options: AppRole — the pod posts a role_id and secret_id retrieved from a sidecar that holds long-lived credentials in a ConfigMap
Kubernetes auth — Vault validates the projected service-account JWT against the cluster's TokenReview API and issues a token bound to a role
TLS certificate auth — the cluster issues each pod a client certificate at admission time and Vault matches it against an allow-list
AWS IAM auth — kubelet exchanges the pod identity for an AWS STS token that Vault then verifies against the AWS STS endpoint
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes auth method validates a pod's projected ServiceAccount JWT (at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`) by calling the cluster's TokenReview API — no pre-provisioned secret is needed because the cluster itself attests the identity. Vault then issues a token bound to a role tied to specific ServiceAccount names and namespaces. AppRole requires the sidecar to already hold a sensitive secret_id, defeating the 'no pre-provisioned credentials' requirement. TLS-cert auth assumes a per-pod cert exists, which is not the case here. AWS IAM auth requires AWS STS credentials, which a generic Kubernetes pod does not automatically possess.

questions.question: An administrator is scripting Vault setup. All auth method tuning (enabling, disabling, configuring roles for userpass, ldap, kubernetes, aws, …) must be POSTed to a consistent URL prefix. Which path prefix does Vault use for auth method configuration?
options: `sys/mounts/auth/` — the same prefix used for mounting secrets engines, scoped via a sub-path
`auth/v1/methods/` — the versioned management endpoint added in Vault 1.0 for auth tuning
`sys/auth/` — the system path under which auth methods are enabled, disabled, and tuned
`config/authn/` — the configuration root for authentication, separate from the system tree
questions.explanation: Auth methods are managed under `sys/auth/` (for example `sys/auth/approle` to enable, `sys/auth/approle/tune` to tune). Once enabled they receive requests under `auth/<method>/...`. `sys/mounts/` is for secrets engines, not auth methods. There is no `auth/v1/methods/` versioned tuning endpoint — Vault's API is unversioned at the URL level. And there is no `config/authn/` namespace; configuration paths sit under each engine or under `sys/`.

questions.question: A high-throughput application creates thousands of Vault tokens per second. Which token type is optimised for this scenario and why?
options: Orphan tokens — they bypass storage because they have no parent token to track in the hierarchy
Service tokens — they cache the parent lookup so high-volume workloads avoid repeated reads
Root tokens — they bypass storage overhead entirely, suitable for high-frequency bootstrap operations
Batch tokens — they are encoded entirely in the token string, not stored in Vault, so creation is cheap
questions.explanation: Batch tokens are encoded entirely in the token string and never written to Vault's storage backend, so creation is extremely cheap — ideal for short-lived, high-volume use (Lambda, CI jobs). They cannot be renewed and cannot have children, which is acceptable in those scenarios. Orphan tokens are still service tokens written to storage; their orphan-ness only affects parent-revocation chains, not throughput. Service tokens require a storage write per creation — exactly the cost batch tokens avoid. Root tokens are not designed for high-frequency creation and are restricted to bootstrap use, not a throughput tool.

questions.question: Which Vault secrets engine is automatically mounted, scoped exclusively to the current token, and used internally for response wrapping?
options: Identity secrets engine, which stores per-entity metadata that response wrapping uses as a transport layer
KV v1 at the `secret/` mount, used by Vault internally to stash wrapped responses for a single token
Cubbyhole secrets engine — always mounted at `cubbyhole/`, private to the current token, and the storage layer behind response wrapping
System secrets engine at `sys/` — exposes a per-token scratch directory used by the wrapping subsystem
questions.explanation: Cubbyhole is always mounted at `cubbyhole/` and is strictly private to each token — no other token can read another's cubbyhole. Response wrapping stores the wrapped secret inside a single-use wrapping token's cubbyhole; when that token is consumed or expires, its cubbyhole and the wrapped data are destroyed together. Identity is a metadata system, not a token-scoped secret store. KV v1 at `secret/` is a shared mount in OSS by default — not per-token, and not the wrapping store. `sys/` is the system API namespace; it is not a per-token KV mount.

questions.question: An operator needs to revoke a specific token without knowing the token's actual value. Which Vault concept allows this?
options: Token accessor — an opaque reference that allows lookup and revocation without the token value itself
Token alias — the per-auth-method identifier linked to the Vault Identity Entity
Token display name — the human label set at creation time for log readability
Token entity ID — the Identity Entity that owns the token across auth methods
questions.explanation: Every Vault token has an accessor — an opaque reference stored in audit logs that allows administrative lookup and revocation via `vault token revoke -accessor <accessor>`, without ever exposing the token value. Aliases are how Identity links an auth-method login to an Entity; they are not used to revoke a token. The display name is a human-readable label for logs; it is not unique and cannot drive revocation. The entity ID identifies the Identity Entity, not a specific token, so revoking by entity would revoke all of that user's tokens, not the one needed.

questions.question: A policy attached to a token reads: `path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }`. The token attempts `vault kv get secret/data/app/db`. Vault allows it. The same token then tries `vault kv put secret/data/app/db @creds.json`. What happens to the write?
options: Allowed — the wildcard glob covers every verb on any matching path, until an explicit deny rule fires elsewhere
Allowed but degraded — the write succeeds and is stored under a quarantine flag pending out-of-band review
Denied — the policy grants only the read capability on that prefix; writing requires `create` or `update` capability
Denied with a token revocation — Vault treats the attempted write as escalation and invalidates the token immediately
questions.explanation: Vault is deny-by-default and capabilities are not implied by each other: a policy that lists only `read` allows only reads. A `kv put` needs `create` (for new keys) or `update` (for existing keys) — neither is granted here, so the write is denied. There is no 'covers every verb' rule in Vault — globs match paths, not capabilities. There is no quarantine flag for writes pending approval. And Vault does not revoke a token just for hitting an ACL denial; it returns a 403 and continues to honour the token within its remaining policy.

questions.question: On a brand-new Vault server with no data, an operator runs a single command that generates the root key, splits it into shares with a configurable threshold, and prints an initial root token. The command can only succeed once on a given cluster. Which operator command is it?
options: `vault operator init` — runs once on a fresh cluster, generates the Shamir shares and initial root token
`vault operator unseal` — accepts key shares one at a time until threshold is reached, then transitions the node from sealed to unsealed
`vault operator generate-root` — uses a quorum of existing key shares to mint a new root token for break-glass on a running cluster
`vault operator rekey` — generates fresh unseal key shares from a quorum of existing shares without invalidating the root key
questions.explanation: `vault operator init` is the one-shot bootstrap: it generates the Shamir key shares and prints an initial root token. It can only succeed once on a given cluster. `vault operator unseal` is run repeatedly (after every restart, once per share) to reconstruct the master key on an already-initialised cluster — it does not create the shares. `vault operator generate-root` mints a new root token on a running cluster and requires a quorum of existing shares; it does not initialise anything. `vault operator rekey` rotates the unseal shares but again requires an existing quorum and is unrelated to first-time init.

questions.question: A team wants to create a Vault policy that allows listing secrets in `secret/team-a/` but prevents reading the secret VALUES. Which capability achieves this?
options: Read capability on the data path with a documented convention that operators only list keys, not values
List capability on the metadata path (`secret/metadata/team-a/*`) without any read on the data path
Sudo capability with the read sub-capability explicitly disabled in the policy stanza
Create capability on `secret/team-a/` so callers can enumerate keys as a side effect of writing
questions.explanation: In KV v2 the metadata and data live at distinct paths: `secret/metadata/team-a/*` is what `list` enumerates, and `secret/data/team-a/*` is where `read` returns the value. Granting only `list` on the metadata path lets a caller see secret names without being able to read their values — a clean KV v2 separation that KV v1 cannot offer. 'Read with a convention' is not enforcement — Vault would let the caller read every value. There is no sub-capability toggle to disable read inside `sudo`. `create` allows writes, not listing, and using a write to enumerate keys is not how listing works in Vault.

questions.question: A regulated bank wants to avoid distributing unseal-key shares to five humans. Instead, on each restart Vault should unseal itself by calling an external key-management service that protects the unseal key under a customer-managed CMK. Which mechanism delivers this?
options: Recovery keys — a parallel set of key shares with reduced privileges, still distributed to the same operators with a smaller share count
Transit auto-unseal via another Vault cluster's Transit engine — works, but defeats the goal because that other cluster still needs a human unseal
Cloud KMS auto-unseal — Vault stores the encrypted root key on the backend and calls AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS to decrypt it at startup
Shamir auto-unseal — Vault performs the secret-sharing reconstruction itself in memory at boot, bypassing the operator quorum entirely
questions.explanation: Auto-unseal with a Cloud KMS (or HSM) lets Vault wrap its root key under a customer-managed CMK and unwrap it on startup, eliminating human key holders. Recovery keys still need humans (just for break-glass operations on an auto-unsealed cluster) and do not replace key holders for the unseal flow itself. Transit auto-unseal is real, but routing to another Vault cluster only shifts the human-quorum problem to the other cluster — the bank's stated goal is not met. 'Shamir auto-unseal' is not a thing — Shamir is the manual quorum scheme, and there is no in-memory auto-reconstruction that bypasses operators.

questions.question: A dynamic database credential was issued with a 1-hour lease. After 10 minutes the operator runs `vault lease revoke <lease_id>` against it. What does Vault do to the underlying database password?
options: Marks the lease revoked in Vault but leaves the database account untouched; the credential remains valid until the engine's next periodic cleanup
Calls the database plugin to DROP or disable the dynamically created account, then deletes the lease metadata — the credential is no longer accepted
Notifies the application via the lease watcher channel, expecting it to issue a fresh request; the password itself is left in place
Rotates the credential's password but keeps the account, so any client still holding the old password is gracefully rejected without losing the user
questions.explanation: Revoking a dynamic database lease triggers immediate revocation at the database: Vault uses its stored admin connection to DROP or disable the user it created for that lease, so the credentials stop being accepted right away. Vault does not just mark the lease revoked and wait for cleanup — that would leave a stolen credential usable. There is no lease-watcher notification channel that Vault calls back to applications. Rotating the password while keeping the account is what a static role does on rotation; for dynamic credentials Vault drops the account itself.

questions.question: A Vault token has a TTL of 1 hour but the application needs it to remain valid for 8 hours. The token's `max_ttl` is 24 hours. What should the application do?
options: Re-authenticate every hour to mint a fresh token, accepting the extra auth-method traffic over the application's lifetime
Enable token immortality by setting TTL to 0 so renewals are no longer needed for the running application
Change the token's TTL using `vault token update` to override the current expiry to the desired horizon
Call `vault token renew` before the TTL expires to extend the token, bounded by `max_ttl`
questions.explanation: Renewable Vault tokens are extended via `vault token renew` (or the API equivalent) — each renewal pushes the expiry forward by the configured increment, bounded by `max_ttl`. Vault Agent automates this. Re-authenticating every hour works but is unnecessarily expensive; renewal is the intended pattern. Setting TTL to 0 does not produce an immortal token — it just uses the system default TTL. There is no `vault token update` command that mutates an existing token's TTL on the fly; you renew it or re-issue.

questions.question: An infrastructure team wants to grant engineers SSH access to ephemeral VMs without distributing long-lived SSH keys. Instead they want Vault to mint a one-time password per host that the host's PAM module validates against Vault. Which secrets engine fits?
options: The PKI engine — Vault signs short-lived X.509 certificates that openssh-server validates via TrustedUserCAKeys, no per-host secret needed
The SSH engine in OTP mode — Vault generates a single-use password per session that the target validates via the vault-ssh-helper PAM plugin
The TOTP engine — Vault stores per-host shared TOTP secrets and engineers compute a 6-digit code locally using their authenticator app
The KV engine with a sidecar — a daemon on each host polls Vault every 60 seconds for the rotating password and updates `/etc/shadow`
questions.explanation: The SSH secrets engine in OTP mode generates a single-use password per user/host pair, which the vault-ssh-helper PAM plugin on the target validates back to Vault — no long-lived SSH keys are distributed. The PKI engine issues X.509 (TLS) certificates, not SSH credentials. The TOTP engine generates time-based 6-digit codes (RFC 6238), not SSH session passwords, and assumes a pre-shared secret with the user. The KV-and-sidecar story is a custom workaround that would leak shadow-file rotations — Vault has a purpose-built engine, so a homegrown approach is the wrong answer.

questions.question: A new client authenticates and receives a token with two policies listed: the application policy and another policy that is automatically attached. The auto-attached policy grants the bare minimum needed for the token to renew itself and look up its own info. Which policy is it?
options: The `root` policy, attached as a fallback when no other policy is named at token creation, granting unrestricted access until tuned later
The `default` policy, attached to every non-root token unless explicitly excluded, granting self-renew, self-lookup, cubbyhole, and a handful of helpers
The `admin` policy, attached automatically so the application can renew its token during a probation window before being demoted to a lower-privilege role
The `audit` policy, attached so the token can write its own audit records to the configured audit devices for forensic replay
questions.explanation: The `default` policy is automatically attached to every non-root token at creation. It grants exactly the self-management permissions a token needs: `auth/token/renew-self`, `auth/token/lookup-self`, `auth/token/revoke-self`, plus its own cubbyhole. It can be excluded with `token_no_default_policy` on an auth role. The `root` policy is never auto-attached — it grants unrestricted access and is reserved for the initial bootstrap token. There is no built-in `admin` policy attached automatically. There is no built-in `audit` policy — audit logging is configured at the device level, not via a per-token policy.

questions.question: A Vault transit key has been rotated (now on version 3). Data was encrypted with versions 1 and 2. How does Vault handle decryption of old ciphertext?
options: Vault automatically re-encrypts all stored data across all old versions with the new key on rotation, so old ciphertext disappears
Old ciphertext can no longer be decrypted after rotation; clients must re-encrypt all data with the new version to keep accessing it
The application must manually specify the key version on every decrypt call, otherwise Vault returns an unknown-version error
Vault keeps every non-deleted key version and decrypts ciphertext using the version embedded in the ciphertext prefix
questions.explanation: Transit ciphertext is prefixed with the key version that produced it (`vault:v1:…`, `vault:v2:…`). Vault keeps every non-deleted version and uses the prefix to pick the right key for decryption — the caller does not need to know the version. Vault does not silently re-encrypt your stored data on rotation (it cannot — it has no copy of your at-rest data). Old ciphertext stays decryptable for as long as the relevant version is retained. The version is read from the ciphertext, not supplied by the client. Old versions can be trimmed deliberately via `transit/keys/<name>/trim`.

questions.question: A Vault HA cluster runs on integrated storage. The operator needs to take a consistent point-in-time backup of the entire data store (encrypted) that can later be restored on a fresh cluster as part of disaster recovery drills. They run a single CLI command that streams the snapshot to a local file. Which command does this?
options: `vault operator raft snapshot save backup.snap` — streams a binary snapshot of the Raft store to a local file for later restore
`vault audit enable file file_path=backup.snap` — exports an append-only log of every operation, which can be replayed against a new cluster
`vault operator rekey -backup snapshot=backup.snap` — exports the current unseal key shares so a quorum can be reconstituted later
`vault operator generate-root -dr backup.snap` — produces a recovery bundle containing the root token and policies for a replacement node
questions.explanation: `vault operator raft snapshot save` streams a binary snapshot of the entire Raft storage (Vault data, policies, auth config, audit settings) to a file. It can be restored on a fresh cluster with `vault operator raft snapshot restore`. Enabling an audit device only writes per-request log lines; it is not a point-in-time backup and replaying audit logs does not reconstruct state. `vault operator rekey` rotates unseal shares — it does not back up data and the `-backup` here is for the new shares, not for storage. `vault operator generate-root` produces a new root token, not a data backup.

questions.question: An AppRole role is configured with `secret_id_num_uses=1`. What happens when a CI/CD system tries to use the same `secret_id` a second time?
options: Vault authenticates successfully but reduces the remaining use count to a negative number to signal over-use to the audit log
Vault grants the authentication and writes a warning to the audit log so operators can rotate the secret_id later
Vault refreshes the secret_id automatically with a new value and returns it to the caller for the second login
Vault rejects the authentication because the secret_id has been consumed and cannot be used again
questions.explanation: `secret_id_num_uses=1` makes a secret_id single-use: after one successful login it is consumed and any further attempt fails. This is the recommended pattern for CI/CD, where each deployment receives a fresh secret_id and burns it. Vault does not allow the second login while logging a warning — it returns an authentication failure. There is no auto-refresh that replaces a consumed secret_id; new secret_ids must be requested explicitly. And use counts never go negative as a signal — Vault simply rejects once the count hits zero.

questions.question: A platform engineer is installing a Vault binary on a fresh host. Before starting the service they create a file the binary reads at startup to learn its listener addresses, storage backend, telemetry, seal stanza, and cluster name. What does that file define?
options: The server configuration file (`vault.hcl`) — defines listener, storage, cluster address, telemetry, and seal stanzas read at process start
The policy bundle — a flattened list of every policy that should exist on the running server, applied automatically when the binary boots
The secrets-engine seed — pre-populates KV mounts with initial values so smoke tests succeed on the first boot of a fresh node
The audit ruleset — declares which paths must be logged and at what verbosity, replacing the runtime `audit enable` command for compliance
questions.explanation: The Vault server configuration file (commonly `vault.hcl`) is read at process start and defines listener, storage, cluster_addr, api_addr, seal (including auto-unseal), and telemetry. It does NOT carry secrets or policies — those are managed via the API/CLI after the server is running. There is no policy-bundle file consumed at boot; policies are created with `vault policy write`. There is no secrets-engine seed file. Audit devices are enabled at runtime via `vault audit enable`, not by a startup ruleset.

questions.question: An administrator is exploring Vault's HTTP API. They notice that mount tuning, health, leader status, audit configuration, license info, and policy management are all reachable under one path prefix that maps to Vault's built-in system endpoint. Which path is it?
options: `internal/` — Vault's reserved namespace for internal cluster traffic and inter-node RPCs
`admin/v1/` — the versioned management endpoint exposed in Vault 1.0 for cluster administration
`sys/` — the system API namespace covering mounts, health, audit, policies, and seal operations
`vault/system/` — the documented system root inherited from early HashiCorp Vault releases
questions.explanation: Vault's system API lives under `sys/`. Examples include `sys/health`, `sys/seal`, `sys/unseal`, `sys/mounts`, `sys/auth`, `sys/policies`, and `sys/audit`. Most operations on `sys/` paths require the `sudo` capability. There is no public `internal/` namespace exposed for administration — internal RPCs are not part of the user-facing HTTP API. There is no `admin/v1/` prefix; Vault's API is unversioned at the URL. There is no `vault/system/` legacy root — historical Vault versions also used `sys/`.

questions.question: A Vault admin wants to provide an external team temporary read access to a specific secret, with the access token self-destructing after delivery. Which mechanism achieves this?
options: Create an IAM user for the team with read-only access scoped narrowly to the relevant Vault path
Enable public access on the secret path temporarily until the external team retrieves the value
Share the root token temporarily so the team can use it for one operation, then revoke it on the admin's side
Use response wrapping — Vault returns a single-use wrapping token that unwraps to the secret and self-destructs
questions.explanation: Response wrapping creates a single-use wrapping token that holds the wrapped secret in the token's cubbyhole. The admin delivers the wrapping token; when unwrapped, the secret is returned and the wrapping token is destroyed. If an interceptor unwraps first, the legitimate recipient sees a 'token used' error — interception is detectable. Creating an IAM user works only for AWS, not as a Vault delivery mechanism. There is no 'public access' toggle for a Vault path — Vault is deny-by-default. Sharing a root token grants unlimited access and is never the right answer in a security-sensitive workflow.

questions.question: A workload requests a token whose lifetime should NOT depend on the lifetime of any other token. When the token that issued the credential expires or is revoked, the new token must survive. To achieve this, the issuing token uses a specific flag at create time. What does that flag set?
options: Creates an orphan token — no parent in the token hierarchy, so it is not revoked when its issuer is revoked; only its own TTL, max_ttl, or explicit revocation ends it
Marks the token as exempt from audit logging for its lifetime, so high-throughput batch jobs do not flood downstream SIEMs while still inheriting the parent's lifecycle
Allows the token to bypass policy checks on a configurable subset of paths to support break-glass operations during an incident response window
Causes the token's TTL to be refreshed every time a child token is created beneath it, effectively pinning the parent's lifetime to its longest-lived child
questions.explanation: By default, revoking a Vault token revokes its entire child tree. An orphan token (created with the orphan flag, or via `auth/token/create-orphan`) has no parent in the hierarchy, so it survives independent of the issuer — only its own TTL, max_ttl, or explicit revocation can end it. There is no flag that exempts a token from audit logging — audit coverage is global. There is no flag that lets a token bypass policy on a subset of paths; bypass requires the root policy. And there is no parent-refreshes-on-child mechanism — child creation does not extend the parent.

questions.question: A Vault audit log shows a request with HMAC-ed token value. Why are token values HMACed in audit logs?
options: To compress the token representation for storage efficiency in long-retention audit archives
To prevent the actual token from being readable while still allowing correlation across log entries
To allow log replay for debugging — operators reverse the HMAC to recover the token when a session must be reproduced
To encrypt the entire audit log entry end-to-end for SOC 2 and PCI compliance regimes
questions.explanation: Vault HMACs sensitive values (tokens, secret values) in audit logs using a per-device salt. The HMAC is one-way, so anyone who reads the logs cannot recover usable tokens, but the same token always hashes to the same HMAC — letting operators correlate calls made by one token across log lines without ever exposing it. HMAC has nothing to do with compression. HMAC is one-way and cannot be reversed by an operator, so log replay via token recovery is impossible by design. HMAC also does not encrypt the whole entry — only the sensitive fields are hashed.

questions.question: On a KV-v2 mount, an operator runs `vault kv delete secret/app/db` then later runs `vault kv destroy -versions=3 secret/app/db`. The first command leaves the data recoverable; the second does not. What is the difference?
options: The first removes the latest version from the listing while keeping earlier versions readable; the second permanently removes the listing entry for every prior version
Both commands permanently remove data that is not recoverable; the only difference is that the second writes an audit record at higher verbosity with no behavioural distinction
The first marks specific versions as soft-deleted (recoverable via `vault kv undelete`); the second permanently wipes the underlying data for the named versions and is irreversible
The first removes only the policy that allows reads, leaving the data intact; the second wipes the data and the policy, requiring re-grant before any further reads
questions.explanation: In KV v2, `vault kv delete` performs a soft-delete: the named version is flagged deleted but the data remains and can be recovered via `vault kv undelete`. `vault kv destroy -versions=…` permanently removes the underlying ciphertext for the listed versions — irreversible. The metadata (version history) still shows the version existed, but the data itself is gone. The 'just removes from listing' framing is wrong — deletion is a soft mark, not a listing manipulation. The two commands do not differ only in verbosity — they have different durability. And neither command touches policies; policies and data are independent.

questions.question: An application runs in AWS EC2. Which Vault auth method allows the EC2 instance to authenticate without any pre-placed secrets?
options: LDAP auth using the EC2 hostname as a directory record matched against a per-region OU
TLS certificate auth using the instance's TLS certificate, mapped to a Vault role by SAN
AppRole with the role_id stored in EC2 user-data and the secret_id fetched from IMDS at boot
AWS auth method using the EC2 instance identity document signed by AWS and fetched from IMDS
questions.explanation: The AWS auth method supports EC2 mode: the instance reads its identity document from IMDS (which is signed by AWS) and posts it to Vault; Vault verifies the signature against AWS's public certificate and binds the login to a role keyed on AMI ID, account, region, or IAM role. LDAP auth requires a directory account, not 'just the hostname'. TLS-cert auth requires the cluster to have already provisioned a client cert to each instance — that is a pre-placed secret. AppRole still requires a sensitive secret_id; storing the role_id in user-data does not remove that requirement.

questions.question: An operator wants to force a controlled leader election on a Vault HA cluster — perhaps to drain the active node before an OS upgrade. They run a CLI command on the active node that causes it to relinquish leadership; another standby is then promoted. Which command does this?
options: `vault operator step-down` — forces the active node to relinquish leadership and triggers an election among the standbys
`vault operator drain` — drains in-flight requests on the active node and queues new requests until a standby is manually promoted via a force-promote call
`vault operator replication pause` — pauses replication to performance-secondary clusters so the active node can complete maintenance without affecting downstream replicas
`vault operator raft promote` — disables the read-replica role on the local node and promotes it to perform an out-of-cluster restore from the latest snapshot
questions.explanation: `vault operator step-down` causes the active Vault node to give up its leadership; a standby then wins the election and becomes active. The stepped-down node remains in the cluster as a standby — used for planned maintenance, rolling upgrades, and failover testing. There is no `vault operator drain` command, and Vault does not queue requests behind a manual promote. `vault operator replication pause` belongs to Enterprise replication; it does not change leadership inside one cluster. `vault operator raft promote` is not a real subcommand — there is no read-replica concept in Vault Raft, and out-of-cluster restore uses `snapshot restore`.

questions.question: Which Vault feature allows path-based routing rules to override or deny access based on contextual information like time of day or IP address? (Enterprise)
options: Vault Sentinel — Endpoint Governing Policies (EGPs) and Role Governing Policies (RGPs) expressed in HashiCorp's Sentinel policy-as-code language
ACL templating in Vault policies — substitutes identity metadata into path strings to make policy decisions contextual
LDAP group-based policy assignment — maps directory groups to Vault policies at login time
Token metadata conditions — restricts what a token can do based on metadata attached at creation time
questions.explanation: Vault Enterprise's Sentinel integration provides Endpoint Governing Policies (EGPs) on specific paths and Role Governing Policies (RGPs) on roles. These use the Sentinel language to express conditions like time-of-day, source IP, or MFA-required — beyond what static ACL capabilities express. ACL templating substitutes identity metadata into paths but cannot evaluate request-time context like IP or wall-clock time. LDAP group binding just attaches policies to logins; it has no contextual filter. Token metadata sits on the token and can be inspected but does not implement path-based routing rules.

questions.question: A team stores secrets at `secret/data/team-a/db`. They want to enforce that only tokens with entity metadata `team=team-a` can access this path. Which Vault ACL template feature enables this?
options: Vault cannot use entity metadata from a token for dynamic policy decisions — only static path prefixes are supported in policies
ACL templating with `{{identity.entity.metadata.team}}` in the policy path string, substituted at evaluation time
AWS IAM condition keys embedded inside Vault policy stanzas to constrain access by tag
LDAP group binding directly to the secret path, so directory membership grants the read capability
questions.explanation: Vault ACL templating evaluates `{{identity.entity.metadata.<key>}}` (and other identity tokens) at policy-evaluation time. A policy like `path "secret/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.team}}/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }` resolves the placeholder against the authenticated entity, so each entity sees only its team's path. Vault definitely supports dynamic policy decisions based on identity metadata, so the 'static prefixes only' claim is wrong. AWS IAM condition keys are not understood by Vault policies. LDAP groups attach to entities via aliases but cannot be bound directly to a path inside a policy.

questions.question: A new operator on a fresh Vault server wants to enable the database secrets engine at a custom path so the team can mint dynamic Postgres credentials. They have access to the host but have not interacted with the API yet. What MUST happen first?
options: The server must be initialised AND unsealed, and the operator must authenticate with a token whose policy grants the required capabilities on `sys/mounts/<path>`
The host must have a working Postgres driver installed locally; the operator cannot enable the engine until the driver handshake succeeds during mount
An audit device must be enabled, because mount operations are rejected on clusters where no audit device has been configured for any path
The license file must declare the database engine in its entitlements bundle, because the engine is gated behind a premium tier even in non-prod
questions.explanation: Before mounting any secrets engine the server must be initialised (`vault operator init` once) and unsealed, and the caller must hold a token whose policy includes `update`/`sudo` on `sys/mounts/<path>`. Only after the mount can the engine be configured (connections, roles). Vault itself does not need a local Postgres driver — the database engine connects out to Postgres over the network, and engine plugins ship inside the Vault binary. There is no requirement to enable an audit device before mounting — audit is configured separately, and mounts work without it (although audit is strongly recommended). The database engine is not Enterprise-gated; it ships in Community Edition.

questions.question: An operator runs `vault token lookup` and sees `renewable: false`. What does this mean for the token lifecycle?
options: The token will never expire because non-renewable tokens are treated as static credentials by the lifecycle subsystem
The token can only be renewed by a holder of the root policy, not by the token itself or by its peers
The token can be renewed but the TTL will not actually increase — the renewal call succeeds without advancing the expiry
The token will expire at its TTL and cannot be extended; the application must authenticate again to obtain a new token
questions.explanation: `renewable: false` means the token cannot be extended with `vault token renew`. When the TTL elapses the token becomes invalid and the application must re-authenticate. Batch tokens are always non-renewable by design, and auth roles can opt out of renewability for service tokens. Non-renewable does not mean immortal — it means 'no extension possible', so expiry still happens at TTL. Root cannot renew a non-renewable token either; the property gates the operation itself. And renewal does not succeed without advancing — on a non-renewable token, the renew call returns an error.

questions.question: What is the vault CLI environment variable used to set the Vault server address so you don't have to pass `-address` on every command?
options: `VAULT_ENDPOINT` — set on the shell to point the CLI at a server, supersedes `-address` when both are provided
`VAULT_URL` — full URL of the Vault API; the CLI parses it for scheme, host, and port at every invocation
`VAULT_ADDR` — canonical environment variable read by the Vault CLI and SDKs for the server address
`VAULT_HOST` — hostname of the Vault server; the CLI prepends `https://` and the default port automatically
questions.explanation: `VAULT_ADDR` is the canonical environment variable for the CLI and SDKs (for example `export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200`). Other commonly used ones are `VAULT_TOKEN`, `VAULT_NAMESPACE`, `VAULT_CACERT`, and `VAULT_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` (not for production). `VAULT_ENDPOINT`, `VAULT_URL`, and `VAULT_HOST` are not Vault environment variables — they sound plausible but are fabricated names; setting them has no effect on the CLI.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure that even if the Vault database is stolen, stored secrets cannot be read. What protects the data at rest in Vault's storage backend?
options: TLS encryption on the Vault API listener — protects in-flight requests so storage cannot be read off the wire
Vault's barrier — encrypts every byte written to the storage backend using the master key derived from the unseal keys
Filesystem permissions on the storage directory — only the Vault user can read the Raft files on disk
The storage backend's native encryption (e.g., S3 SSE) — relies on the backend, transparent to Vault
questions.explanation: Vault's cryptographic barrier encrypts every byte written to the storage backend using the master key (reconstructed from the unseal key shares). An attacker who copies the Raft files, Consul KV, or DynamoDB rows still has only ciphertext — that is why Vault starts 'sealed' and refuses to serve until unsealed. TLS protects requests in transit, not data at rest. Filesystem permissions delay but do not stop a root-level theft of the files. Backend-native encryption (S3 SSE, DynamoDB at-rest) is independent of Vault and is no substitute for the barrier — the backend would happily hand the plaintext-from-the-backend-perspective ciphertext-from-Vault's-perspective to anyone with backend credentials.

questions.question: A token is issued with TTL=1h and max_ttl=24h. The application renews the token roughly every 45 minutes while it is running. Which TWO statements about its lifetime are accurate? (select two)
options: Each renewal can extend the token's expiry by up to TTL=1h from the renewal moment, but never past max_ttl=24h from initial creation
Renewals reset both TTL and max_ttl, so a long-running process can keep the same token alive indefinitely with periodic renewals
After 24 hours from creation the token expires regardless of how recently it was renewed; the application must authenticate again to obtain a fresh token
The token enters a grace period after expiry during which it can still authorise reads but is rejected for any write operation against any path
questions.explanation: max_ttl is the hard ceiling on total lifetime from creation, and Vault honours it regardless of renewals. As the token approaches max_ttl the renewal grant shrinks (Vault returns less than the requested TTL). Statements 0 and 2 capture this correctly: renewals push expiry forward by up to TTL but never past max_ttl, and once max_ttl elapses the token is gone. The 'renewals reset max_ttl' claim is wrong — max_ttl is immutable for the life of the token, which is what prevents an immortal token. The 'grace period for reads only' claim is also wrong — Vault does not split expired tokens into read-allowed and write-blocked; once expired the token is rejected on every path.
